posts.title: The 20th, not the 21st: why closing day matters
posts.excerpt: Closing your monthly payroll timecards on the 20th creates the essential five-day buffer needed to verify hours, resolve discrepancies, and ensure every employee is paid accurately on the 25th.
posts.content:
In small business management, the monthly closing day often feels like a moving target. When an owner manages twelve or thirty employees, daily operational demands—from client deliveries to unexpected shift absences—tend to push payroll administration toward the end of the month. Many employers attempt to close their attendance records on the 22nd or even the 24th, leaving less than twenty-four hours to calculate gross earnings, verify overtime, deduct social contributions, and disburse wages. Over the past twelve years running Getsuji Payroll in Ghent, we have consistently observed that shifting the closing day from the 21st to the 20th is the single most effective operational change a small firm can make.

The logic of closing on the 20th rests on a simple principle: calculation accuracy requires deliberate space. At our bureau on Weverslaan, our standard calendar is fixed for about 60 client firms. Timecards close on the 20th. On the 21st and 22nd, our clerks conduct thorough checks and raise any questions regarding unusual absences, doctor certificates, or travel expense allowances. On the 23rd, the business owner reviews and approves the finalized calculation register. On the 25th, salaries arrive in employee bank accounts alongside clean digital payslips. On the last working day of the month, statutory social contributions and tax filings are submitted to Belgian authorities.

When an employer attempts to close on the 21st instead of the 20th, that vital checking window collapses. Payroll is not merely an automated mathematical conversion; it is a legal and human audit. Every pay cycle involves variable real-world factors: an employee who traded shifts without an updated timecard, an unresolved medical absence, or a mid-month change in withholding tax status. When raw hours arrive on the 21st, our team has only forty-eight hours to resolve ambiguities before owner sign-off on the 23rd. If an owner is stuck in a production emergency or offsite client meeting, questions sit unanswered, and the entire schedule is pushed into late-night guesswork.

Closing on the 20th also protects our standard two-person check on every run. At Getsuji Payroll, no calculation sheet is ever sent to an owner without being independently audited by a second colleague. Senior clerk Tomás Verbeek may assemble the shift figures for Marc Janssens at Janssens Bakery, but Pieter Claes or Ines Duarte cross-checks each gross-to-net deduction, overtime multiplier, and sectoral contribution code before the summary is released. That second pair of eyes requires time. Rushing the audit to meet a compressed 24-hour deadline invites transcription errors that erode employee trust and generate costly corrections.

Furthermore, the calendar must accommodate the calendar itself. If the 25th falls on a Saturday or Sunday, Belgian banking practice requires salary disbursement on the preceding Friday. When the 25th is a Sunday, payday moves to Friday the 23rd, meaning owner approval must occur on the 22nd. Without a strict closing on the 20th, an upcoming weekend payday would leave literally zero working hours to audit attendance. Setting the boundary on the 20th ensures that every employee receives their exact wage on time, every month, without an administrative crisis.

posts.title: Holiday pay in the month someone leaves
posts.excerpt: What goes into a final payslip when a colleague leaves, and which details the bureau needs from you before the 20th.
posts.content:
When a member of staff leaves, the final payslip carries more than the last weeks of wages. Accrued holiday that has not been taken is settled, notice periods are checked against the contract, and any outstanding expenses are added. Each of these needs a date and a number, and none of them can be guessed.

The most helpful thing an owner can do is tell us about the leaver as early as possible, with the last working day and the leave balance as the firm records it. We charge a flat €25 per starter or leaver change, so there is no reason to wait for the 20th to mention it.

On the 21st and 22nd we check the figures against the contract and come back with questions if something does not match. On the 23rd the owner sees the final payslip alongside the rest of the run.

posts.title: What the two-person check is, and why we never skip it
posts.excerpt: How a second clerk reads every pay run before it is released, and what exactly that second reader looks for.
posts.content:
Every pay run at Getsuji Payroll is prepared by one clerk and read by another before the owner is asked to approve it. The second reader does not repeat the calculation from scratch; they look at what changed since last month and at everything that looks unusual: a new starter, a bonus, a rate that moved, a total that differs from the usual by more than it should.

In practice this takes around twenty minutes per firm. Pieter Claes usually reads the runs that involve social contributions and tax filing, and Hana Morel reads the ones with unusual wage structures. If the reader has a question, it goes back to the named clerk, and from the clerk to you.

We do not promise that nothing can ever go wrong. We promise that no run is released that only one person has seen.
